extracted.intended_audience: general readers and fans of television/comedy (also useful background for comedy writers/producers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for producing and evaluating live, late-night sketch comedy as exemplified by Saturday Night Live — covering live performance norms, casting, broadcast standards, digital distribution, and commercial tie-ins. Useful for writers, performers, and producers working in ensemble live-sketch television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lip-Sync An 'SNL' No-No
rubrics_metrics.description: Michaels: Lip-Sync An 'SNL' No-No (reference to Lorne Michaels' stance and coverage such as 'Michaels: Lip-Sync An 'SNL' No-No').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SNL has an explicit expectation of live performance authenticity; lip‑syncing is treated as unacceptable (illustrated by the Ashlee Simpson lip‑sync controversy and attendant criticism). Performers should sing/perform live when required by the show format to avoid reputational and broadcast issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live Broadcast / Airing Live Coast-to-Coast
rubrics_metrics.description: SNL airs live and has staged special live broadcasts (e.g., 'SNL to Air Live in All Time Zones for First Time Ever'; 'To Continue Airing Live Coast To Coast').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches and performances must be timed and staged for live transmission; production must plan for time‑zone differences, possible delays, and the logistics of performing in a live broadcast environment (including contingencies for sports pre‑emptions or schedule changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast Standards and Censorship (Profanity/F-Bombs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage of incidents such as 'Sam Rockwell Drops Surprise "F-Bomb" on "SNL"' and 'Accidental F-Bomb Challenge NBC Censors'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators must account for network decency rules and the risk of live slips: profanity and unexpected language can trigger censorship issues and headlines. Writers and performers should balance edginess with live broadcast constraints and legal/affiliate standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Plagiarism / Maintaining Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: References like '5 sketches that "SNL" allegedly plagiarized' highlight allegations of unoriginal material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear authorship and originality for sketches; plagiarism allegations damage reputation and can lead to public controversy. Vet sketches for originality and proper attribution where material may overlap with other creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting Diversity and Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple references to SNL's diversity record (e.g., long lack of Asian players, only eight Black women in 50 years, first nonbinary cast member, hiring milestones and criticisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting decisions are scrutinized for racial, gender, and LGBTQ+ representation. Producers and hiring teams should consider inclusive recruitment and diverse representation both on stage and in the writers' room to address criticism and better reflect audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting Talent for Past Offensive Remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents such as the Shane Gillis hiring/firing and resurfaced racist/homophobic remarks show consequences of past content ('New "SNL" hire Shane Gillis exposed in videos using racist and homophobic slurs').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers and hires should be vetted for prior public remarks, recorded content, and social media; undisclosed offensive material can lead to immediate backlash, firing, or reputation harm. Production should implement background checks and consider the potential for resurfaced past material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Satire Impact and Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements and reporting that 'SNL' political skits can influence voters and have real impacts ('The SNL Effect: Political Skits Make Real Impact on Voters').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and producers should be aware of the real-world influence of political satire; choices about targets, portrayal, and booking political figures carry consequences. Editorial decisions (e.g., whether to book or parody certain candidates) may be guided by considerations of impartiality, impact, and network policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for Commercialization and Brand Tie-Ins
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of sketches spawning products or brand collaborations (e.g., Ben & Jerry's 'Schweddy Balls' ice cream, other SNL-themed flavors and merchandise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful sketches can lead to merchandising, branded tie‑ins, and commercial opportunities; creators should consider trademark/IP, brand sensitivity (R-rated content may limit retail distribution), and partnership opportunities when producing memorable characters or ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital Distribution and Viral Content Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage of SNL's digital shorts and online impact (e.g., 'Lazy Sunday' and its role in YouTube's rise; global YouTube live streams of big episodes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content creators should plan for online distribution and viral potential: digital shorts, clips, and streaming can vastly extend reach and influence. Consider rights clearance, platform strategies, and how internet virality interacts with television broadcast goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance Quality: Impressions, Monologues, and Strong Debuts
rubrics_metrics.description: References noting when newcomers 'make good, strong impressions' and critiques of monologues (e.g., 'monologue that avoids the obvious').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of cast members often hinge on the strength of character impressions, monologue delivery, and ability to create memorable bits. Casting and promotion decisions may rely on these performance indicators; writers should craft material that allows performers to showcase distinctive voices and impressions.
